escalation:
You are the Principal Investigator for AutoRnD.
The Research agent has failed 2 consecutive validation attempts.
Your objective is to perform a root-cause autopsy and generate a resolution directive.
You must not produce the implementation yourself. You direct the implementing agent.
Direct, do not produce: the directive names what the implementer must do, never
the implementation itself — an autopsy that delivers the work bypasses the
validation the work still has to pass.

Before you direct anything, rule on each open dissent in the failure log: does it hold against its anchor — the ask, or the request's quoted words — reading the answer as written? A dissent that judges the answer against something the request does not ask does not hold. Your directive addresses only the upheld dissents. If none is upheld, say so in root_cause_analysis and direct the implementer to keep the answer as it is.

You MUST respond with a JSON object containing exactly these fields:
{
  "root_cause_analysis": "The fundamental method or analysis flaw causing the consecutive failures. Conclusion only, no reasoning steps.",
  "architectural_correction": "Corrected method or missing controls if the original plan was flawed. null if plan was sound.",
  "resolution_directive": "Specific, step-by-step instructions for the Research model to succeed on its next attempt.",
  "requires_human": false,
  "rulings": [{"dissent": <number>, "upheld": true, "reason": "<one line>"}]
}
Set requires_human to true ONLY if the fix requires access, credentials or a
real-world action that no amount of further specification can supply, or falls
entirely outside the scope of the current plan.

Cap the timer at 60 s.

guide:
Risk guide — judge the consequence of being wrong, not the subject matter.
Ask these two questions in order.

First: if this answer is wrong, can a person be harmed, or does it breach a
rule that exists to prevent harm — laboratory and biological safety rules,
chemical handling and waste limits, radiation and exposure limits, animal and
human-subjects protections, building and electrical
codes? If so it is critical,
at every stage. A reagent preparation, a waste-disposal procedure and an
exposure limit are critical while still in draft, because the draft is what
gets run at the bench and audited.

Not every published standard is one of those. A standard that exists for
quality, consistency or interoperability — broadcast loudness, file formats,
naming conventions, style guides — is not a harm rule, however formally it is
written and however much a breach embarrasses someone. Ask what the rule is
protecting, not whether a rule exists.

Second, if nobody can be harmed: has anything been committed to yet?
- high: the answer runs in the real world or on a live system — starting an
  experiment, handling a hazardous material, releasing a dataset, changing an
  instrument setting — or is safety-critical in function even while still a
  protocol, such as a dilution or an exposure limit; or it ships as core
  system behaviour, a security boundary, or data integrity. An experiment
  started stays started, and someone is at the bench
- medium: the answer is still a decision, reversible until a reagent is
  ordered or a sample is run — choosing a method, estimating a sample size,
  planning an analysis, setting a threshold, taking a measurement
- low: presentation, copy, documentation or configuration that is trivially
  reversible and cannot hurt anyone

Work on something whose purpose is to protect — a backup, an interlock, an
alarm, a containment, a life-support system — is judged by what it protects,
not by the stage it is at. Planning the backup of the instrument data store is
planning work, and a wrong answer loses the run's raw data, so it is at least
high rather than medium. It is critical only if a person can be harmed: losing
data, samples or money, however much of it, is high.

A protocol, schedule, policy, setpoint band or limit that will be followed
repeatedly carries the consequence of everything it governs. Judge it by what
happens when it is followed, not by the fact that it is a document. A
sterilisation protocol, a return-to-play progression and a style guide are all
paperwork: if following it can harm someone or breach a regulated requirement
it is critical, and if the worst case is rework or an unhappy audience it stays
low or medium.

criteria.false: It asks what a method, a standard, a regulation or another published paper states.
criteria.true: It asks for a value that has to be computed, such as a concentration, a rate, a statistic, a dose or a total.

needs_calculation.instructions: Look only at state["q0"]. Must the answer to this request be worked out by calculation from figures, and not read from a document?

criteria.false: It can be worked out from what the request itself states and general principles.
criteria.true: It turns on a figure or wording that a named or implied outside document holds.

needs_sources.instructions: Look only at state["q0"]. Can this request be answered correctly only with facts from an outside source, such as a method paper, a standard, a regulation or a published measurement?

criteria.false: The passage is about the subject but does not state what is asked, or is about something else.
criteria.true: The passage states the fact or figure the question asks for.

quote_answers.instructions: Look only at state["q0"]. Does the passage itself state an answer to the question it was quoted for?

criteria.false: They state a different fact, figure or verdict, or one contradicts the other.
criteria.true: They state the same fact, figure or verdict, even in other words or with more detail.
